planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in evenly moist, well-drained loam; site out of the hottest full-sun exposure to limit leaf scorch and winter bronzing on the variegated foliage.

directions: Variegata is a dense, slow-growing, mounded form of common boxwood whose dark green leaves carry irregular creamy-yellow margins, a distinct look from the crisper white edging of 'Elegantissima' or the blotched gold centers of 'Aureovariegata'. Its compact habit and fine texture suit it to low hedging, edging, and container use where a touch of brightness is wanted without losing the formal boxwood silhouette. Variegated shoots occasionally revert to solid green and should be pruned out to keep the plant from losing its coloring over time. Good drainage and airflow help reduce susceptibility to boxwood blight and root rot in humid climates.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, evenly moist loam; this Michigan-origin selection, documented in a 1945 Weller Nursery catalog, was valued for carrying good green winter color farther north than many English boxwood forms.

directions: Welleri is an older common boxwood selection, documented in a 1945 Weller Nursery Co. catalog from Holland, Michigan, grown for a broad, rounded habit and foliage that holds a cleaner green through winter than many sempervirens cultivars prone to bronzing in cold exposure. It responds well to shearing into a tidy dome or low hedge, and its improved cold tolerance made it a useful English-boxwood-type choice for gardeners at the colder edge of the species' range. Provide good drainage and airflow to minimize boxwood blight and leafminer pressure.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in evenly moist, well-drained loam in full sun to partial shade; this cold-hardy American boxwood selection is also sold under the fuller name 'Elizabeth H. Inglis', formally registered by Saunders Brothers of Piney River, Virginia in 1985.

directions: Inglis forms a dense, pyramidal plant with dark green foliage, growing larger over time than many of the dwarf English boxwood selections and better suited to specimen or screening use than low edging. The name dates back to a 1957 description by Donald Wyman in Arnoldia, and the cultivar was later formally registered as 'Elizabeth H. Inglis' by Saunders Brothers nursery in Piney River, Virginia in 1985. Shear in late winter or after the spring flush to maintain a formal pyramidal or rounded outline, and ensure good drainage and air circulation to reduce risk of boxwood blight and root rot.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in evenly moist, well-drained loam in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Memorial was selected from an old planting at a Williamsburg, Virginia cemetery and registered by John T. Baldwin Jr. in The Boxwood Bulletin in 1967, propagated as a compact, rounded common boxwood with dense, dark green foliage that shows less winter bronzing than many other sempervirens forms. Given time it develops into a substantial rounded mound well suited to foundation plantings, screening, or specimen use, and like other English-type boxwoods it tolerates fairly heavy shearing if a more formal outline is wanted. Provide consistent moisture and good air circulation to reduce susceptibility to boxwood blight and root rot in humid regions.
